extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of aesthetics, poetry, and the fine arts; advanced readers of literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Aristotelian criteria for producing or evaluating fine art (poetry, music, dance, painting, sculpture, drama), focused on imitation, medium-specific expressive capacities, and the relation of art to nature and human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of the useful arts / art supplements nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of the useful arts is in all cases 'to supply the deficiencies of nature'; the master in any art must first discern the true end by a study of nature's principles, and then employ the method which she suggests for the attainment of that end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should both supplement what nature lacks and follow nature's guidance—study natural principles to determine ends and adopt methods suggested by nature. (Illustrated by Milton's and Dante's echoes of the Aristotelian idea.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of aesthetic imitation (threefold)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual objects of aesthetic imitation are threefold — characters (êthê), passions (emotions/moods), and actions (deeds, incidents, situations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic imitation chiefly seeks inward processes (psychical energy, dispositions of the mind) rather than mere external events; deeds count insofar as they spring from an inward act or elicit thought/feeling. Landscape and animals are not primary objects unless they enter human life and heighten human interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as likeness, not mere symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art is a likeness (eikõn/εἰκὼν) or reproduction of an original, and not a symbolic representation of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between conventional symbols (spoken/written words) and mental impressions/portraits: art's images are likenesses stamped on the mind (phantasms) that address sensibility and imagination rather than being arbitrary signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art presents appearances to the senses (aesthetic semblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art reproduces its original not as it is in itself but as it appears to the senses; art addresses the sensibility and image-making faculty and employs illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because art works with appearances and illusions, it must be skilled in creating them so as to give coherence and an air of reality to its fictions. This doctrine leads to the guideline that the poet 'ought to prefer probable impossibilities to possible improbabilities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of imagination / phantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination (phantasy) is an image-forming faculty — the after-effect of sensation — by which we recall pictures previously presented to the mind; for Aristotle it is not a separate creative faculty that recombines materials into wholly new worlds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic invention, on this account, depends on the spontaneous union of intellect and sense; the artist works from images provided by perception and memory rather than from an unconstrained creative imagination that forges entirely novel combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-appropriateness: music as imitation of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Music was held to be the most 'imitative' or representative of the arts: in rhythms and melodies we have realistic imitations of anger, mildness, courage, temperance and their opposites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music's ethical and imitative power lies in rhythm and melody; rhythm especially has an affinity with the movements of the soul, so music can directly influence and form character even apart from words. In Greek practice music was subordinate to poetry and derived much of its meaning from associated words/occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-appropriateness: poetry relies on words to evoke images
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry produces its effects through symbols (words) that call up images; its essence lies in imitation of the idea rather than in metrical form alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though poetry uses conventional signs, these are the natural, familiar media of revealing thought and feeling; metre is neither necessary nor sufficient for poetic quality — imitation of life/idea is primary, and prose can be 'poetic' when it achieves that imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-appropriateness: painting and sculpture (visual signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting and sculpture primarily render outward and physical features and convey moral/spiritual facts largely by signs; yet gestures, facial expressions, and symmetry are natural signs through which the body reflects the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual arts fix a single typical moment which stands representative of a larger action; they should exploit natural, not merely conventional, signs (expression, posture, colour, form, symmetry-as-rhythm) to suggest inner life while recognising limits in depicting successive mental states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-appropriateness: dance as imitative art
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancing imitates character, emotion, and action; the dancer must be perspicuous (understood though silent) and expressive (heard though says nothing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The successful dancer requires genius, critical judgment, comprehensive memory, acquaintance with myth and history, and technical mastery to avoid 'terrible solecisms'; dance harmonises the spectator and trains moral sympathies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of subject matter: focus on human life
rubrics_metrics.description: The common source for all arts is human life — its mental processes, spiritual movements, and outward acts issuing from deeper sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should not treat the whole universe as raw material; external world elements (landscape, animals, objects) are included only insofar as they form a background to, or heighten, human action and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama's central object: action (plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Action are the objects imitated by the arts — by all arts and most obviously by dramatic or narrative poetry; in drama the poetic imitation of life attains its perfect form where action is rendered by action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works should prioritize coherent action (plot) grounded in inner motivations and mental processes rather than mere spectacle or disconnected events; actions may be momentary yet expressive of an inner condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for internal plausibility (probability) in invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'ought to prefer probable impossibilities to possible improbabilities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventing, choose events that are consistent and psychologically or aesthetically probable within the work's world (even if impossible in reality) rather than events that are possible in reality but highly unlikely or unconvincing in context.
